title: My AI workflow shipped a dead feature for 18 months and neither of us noticed. I'm a Navy nuke vet who can't code — here's what I changed.
author: Brehmdig
selftext:
I'm a Navy nuke vet. I ran reactor systems for a living. I could not code.

https://preview.redd.it/a5ho0lofoslh1.png?width=2560&format=png&auto=webp&s=4042ee5348b6ad9f48984d59ec87e18cc05a74c1

**How it failed the first time.**

In early 2025, "using AI" meant a chat window. You couldn't hand it a folder. I'd paste in a chunk, get a chunk back, paste it into my file, run it, watch it break, paste the error back. Four failure modes stacked on top of each other:

1. **It had no context.** It could see thirty lines. It could not see the other four thousand, so it confidently broke things it didn't know existed.
2. **I couldn't verify anything.** I can't read code. So I couldn't tell a working change from a plausible-looking one. My only test was "does it launch."
3. **Nothing was ever proven.** No tests. A bug that didn't crash the game was invisible to me, forever.
4. **I was the bottleneck and I was blind.** Every decision routed through the one person in the loop who couldn't evaluate the work.

One January day I iterated the top bar of my UI **sixteen times** — because I had no way to judge whether any version was better, only whether it looked different. Two days later I quit that project forever.

**The autopsy, 18 months later.**

This month I dug the old prototype out of the archive and pointed my current setup at it. The vacuum upgrade — one people were spending currency on — had never worked. Not once, for anyone. It multiplied by a variable that didn't exist. A player reported the symptom in my itch comments in March 2025. I asked them for a console screenshot and never solved it. The autopsy took about a minute.

That's what building blind actually costs. Not "the AI wrote bad code." I shipped a dead feature for a year and a half because **nothing in my process could tell me it was dead.**

**What I changed.**

Two things, and only one of them was the tools getting better.

The tooling part: models can hold a whole codebase now. Not snippets — the folder. That kills failure mode #1 outright.

The part that was on me: **I stopped trying to be the coder and started being the operator.** I don't read the diff. I demand proof. Concretely:

* Agents implement. **Different agents, with an adversarial brief, try to prove the implementation wrong** — re-deriving math independently, measuring actual rendered pixels, diffing behavior against the previous build frame by frame.
* They fail things. Regularly. One of my biggest systems got sent back and rebuilt because its own review measured it delivering **2–11%** of the damage it claimed. I never would have caught that by looking at it.
* Every fix ships with a test that reproduces its original bug forever. The economy has a conservation law that gets checked every build.
* When I can't verify a claim, it doesn't ship as verified. It ships flagged.

https://preview.redd.it/n4coy8kposlh1.png?width=2559&format=png&auto=webp&s=65fdaee9c21113937eaa1aec5817352b08f51fa6

Same guy, same inability to read code. The difference is that the process now catches what I can't see, instead of relying on me to see it.

My definition after living both sides: **slop is what ships unverified.** I shipped plenty of unverified work with my own two hands and it was much worse than anything I make now.

Free demo went up today if you want to poke at the result. Happy to get into the harness, the adversarial setup, or the failure modes in comments — that's the part I actually like talking about.

[https://store.steampowered.com/app/4985040/Symbiosis\_Criticality/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4985040/Symbiosis_Criticality/)

comments.author: solitaryprawn
comments.body:
It's nice to see that others are dealing with the same concerns that I'm learning about now. I can't code either. I can read it to a degree, but can't write it. Just like I can read French and get the gist but not speak it. 
I've been breaking down my game idea into systems, explaining exactly what I want the system to do and start off with basic functionality. Then add on to it, test it, fix it and repeat. I've also noticed improvements on the AI side. Less errors, less forgotten function names. There's an ability there now to remember or at least be aware of the rest of the code. 
I'm extremely glad that this new tool exists and that actually learning to use it improves results instead of using it as an "easy button"
Also, Navy nuke sounds really cool. I'm just a naval missile system technician.

comments.author: No-Pollution7797
comments.body:
The adversarial-review harness is the right shape, but there's a sibling failure mode it won't catch, and it's the one that got us.

Your vacuum upgrade multiplied by a variable that didn't exist. That's a wrong answer. The nastier version is a *plausible* answer — code that fails and returns something that looks like a legitimate result.

Ours: a sitemap builder that queried the DB for published items, wrapped in a try/catch that returned an empty array on failure. In one build the DB env var wasn't present at that point in the pipeline, the query threw, the catch swallowed it, and the function returned []. Everything downstream was happy. No crash, no red build, tests green. 23 items silently dropped out of our sitemap and stayed gone for weeks. An adversarial reviewer asked to "prove this implementation wrong" would have read that function and correctly concluded it was fine — because it *was* fine. The bug was in what it did when it failed.

Two things that actually moved the needle for us:

**Ban the silent fallback.** Any catch that returns a neutral value — empty list, zero, null, "unknown" — has to log loudly first. We now literally leave a comment at those sites saying what went wrong last time, because the next person's instinct is to quiet it down again.

**Assert non-triviality, not just correctness.** Most assertions ask "is the output right?" and an empty output passes trivially. The ones that earn their keep ask "is the output non-empty / within a plausible band?" Your economy conservation law is already exactly this instinct — it can't be satisfied by nothing happening. Generalizing that to "every generated collection has a floor" is cheap and catches a whole class of invisible deaths.

Related: your "ships flagged when unverifiable" rule is the part I'd steal. The failure isn't usually that someone lied about verification — it's that unverified and verified look identical three months later when you're deciding what to trust.
